analysis.title: 2027 Global Market Outlook: Growth Without Goldilocks
key_insights: Base case for the Middle East is a 'prolonged quagmire' between the U.S. and Iran, with oil at $90-120 per barrel. PGIM puts the risk of resumed all-out war at 30% as of October 2026, which would push oil well above $120.
Geopolitics, trade frictions and AI-buildout supply pressures are driving high and volatile inflation. PGIM expects central banks to treat this as a warning for inflation expectations.
PGIM expects the Trump administration to use executive orders to raise the average U.S. tariff rate from about 10% to closer to 15%, given likely legislative gridlock in 2027.

PGIM sees the AI buildout mainly as a global demand story, not yet a productivity story. Hyperscaler capex in 2026 could add up to one percentage point to U.S. real GDP growth, with a modestly smaller impulse in 2027.
The U.S. base case is an overheating economy, with growth above potential and inflation above the Fed's 2% target. U.S. domestic demand exceeds domestic production, with imports filling the gap.

Sovereign debt issuance now competes with heavy AI-related corporate issuance for the same pool of global savings. France is Europe's weakest fiscal link, with spreads over Bunds the highest in the euro area, above Italy and Greece.

PGIM's base case for France is muddle-through with some EU forbearance, but the situation will stay fluid for 6-12 months until a new government and budget are in place. U.S. deficits run 6-8% of GDP against France's 5-6%.

PGIM expects another 100 bps of Fed tightening, taking the terminal Fed funds rate to 5%, with the next hike in December 2026 and a quarterly pace after. Higher rates raise U.S. recession probability from historically low levels to near the historical average of about 25%.

PGIM expects the ECB to hike one last time, to 2.75%. The BoJ is expected to hike in December and twice more by 25 bps, taking the policy rate to 1.75%, the midpoint of its 1.0-2.5% neutral range. The PBoC is expected to stay accommodative.
The report describes a converging hiking cycle across major central banks, with policy rate risks tilted to the upside and a possibility that central banks hike until something breaks.

Scenario probabilities differ by region. The U.S. base case is strong growth with recession as the main downside. Euro area base case is 40% with energy-driven mild stagflation as the main downside. China base case is 65%. Emerging markets base case is muddle through at 37%.

Fixed income: PGIM prefers selective carry over long duration, favoring short and intermediate maturities, short-maturity high yield, AAA CLOs and AAA RMBS. It stays cautious on long duration over 12 months and expects four more 25 bp Fed hikes in the next 12 months.

Credit spreads, adjusted for duration and quality, are near historical tights. PGIM keeps a defensive view on investment grade and is only marginally more constructive on global leveraged finance. It prefers U.S. to Europe in leveraged finance. CCCs and hyperscaler bonds have underperformed.

Higher rates need not derail risk assets. U.S. equity returns show low sensitivity to rising Treasury yields, and since 2000 high yield and EM debt excess returns over government debt have been positive when yields rose. AI investment is also relatively insensitive to rates.

Equities: PGIM expects data center capex above $800 billion in 2026 and $1 trillion in 2027. AI equities rose in Q2 2026 and reversed in Q3 on momentum reversals and hedge-fund liquidations while earnings and estimates kept rising. Semiconductors stay central, with opportunities in the Asian supply chain, memory, cloud services, power equipment and grid technology.

PGIM favors cybersecurity within software and sees AI-native platforms possibly gaining share from older software models. It also favors aerospace and power-related industrials that benefit from long-lived capacity constraints.

Private credit has tripled since 2010 to more than $3 trillion. PGIM is constructive on asset-based finance, infrastructure debt, private placements and senior direct lending in the middle market, and selective on digital infrastructure and compute finance. It warns premia could narrow in large-cap direct lending and IG private placements.

Real estate is in an extended early-cycle phase. Data centers have the strongest return prospects of any real estate sector. PGIM favors core and high-yield real estate credit and defensive grocery-anchored retail, and expects entry points to stay attractive given low liquidity.

sector_views.rationale: Compute demand exceeds capacity. Opportunities extend to the Asian supply chain, memory, cloud services, power equipment and grid technology.
They benefit from long-lived capacity constraints.
Needs greater discrimination. Cybersecurity is well positioned and AI-native platforms may gain share from older software models.
Scarce capacity and power constraints support persistent rental growth. PGIM sees the strongest return prospects of any real estate sector.
Spreads are historically tight, so PGIM favors carry over spread compression, with exposure to money center banks, electric utilities, midstream pipelines and AI-related deals.
Term premium pressure from fiscal risk, heavy corporate issuance and inflation uncertainty.

earnings_insights: PGIM says earnings are strong and estimates are rising across the AI complex, with cloud revenue accelerating at Google, Amazon and Microsoft. The report gives no specific EPS or revenue figures.
PGIM says equity earnings and guidance are improving while valuations decline, so the question is whether the long-term investment thesis has changed. It judges that the evidence says it has not.

trade_ideas.description: Favor short-maturity high yield credit in developed and emerging markets, and AAA CLOs, over long-duration bonds
trade_ideas.rationale: Carry is attractive without taking excessive credit or duration risk.
trade_ideas.risk: Spreads are near historical tights, so selectivity is needed.

trade_ideas.description: Stay in short and intermediate fixed income rather than the long end of the yield curve
trade_ideas.rationale: Term premium pressure from fiscal risk, heavy corporate issuance and inflation uncertainty makes long duration a source of volatility.
trade_ideas.risk: A peak in rates could favor long duration.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight AI supply-bottleneck equities: semiconductors, memory, Asian supply chain, power equipment, grid technology
trade_ideas.rationale: Compute demand exceeds capacity and supply is constrained by chips, power generation and grid infrastructure.
trade_ideas.risk: Debate over durability and returns on AI capital, financing circularity, and political resistance to data centers.

trade_ideas.description: Own aerospace and power-related industrials and U.S. power and energy credit
trade_ideas.rationale: Long-lived capacity constraints support these businesses.

risk_factors: Resumed all-out war in the Middle East, which PGIM puts at 30% and which would send oil well above $120.
A late-winter cold snap pushing European gas prices and euro area inflation above the expected 4% peak.
A Fed overtightening or an AI-driven demand shock causing a U.S. recession.
A Treasury repricing triggered by an economic slowdown, added fiscal spending after the midterms, or debt-ceiling brinkmanship in 2027.
French fiscal and political stress spreading to Belgium, Italy and European corporates, with the ECB's intervention bar likely high.
An upside overshoot in Japanese yields as the BoJ hikes faster.
Hyperscaler issuance saturating credit markets and a questioning of AI returns on capital.
A hiking cycle that continues until something breaks, with inflation and policy rate risks tilted to the upside.
Dispersion and tail risk in private credit, with lower tranches of rated feeders, CLOs and risk transfer deals potentially showing stress first.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 plots the real GDP contribution from data centers as Q2 moving averages in percentage points, 2022 to Q2 2026.
Exhibit 9 plots the French 10-year spread to Bunds against Italy, Spain, Greece and U.S. and euro aggregate OAS, January to October 2026, in basis points.
Exhibit 11 shows forecast incremental AI data center power demand rising from 13 GW in 2025 to 59 GW in 2030E.
vol_and_positioning: AI equities reversed in Q3 2026 on momentum reversals, hedge-fund liquidations and broader risk reduction, which compressed valuations despite rising estimates.
Credit spreads remain near the narrow end of their historical ranges despite recent volatility. Global wealth investors have so far not panic-sold as rates rose.
Term structures may consolidate around late-October levels. PGIM warns that BoJ hikes could produce an upside yield overshoot with global ramifications.
geopolitical: U.S.-Iran conflict in the Middle East: PGIM's base case is a prolonged quagmire, with a 30% risk of resumed all-out war as of October 2026.
The Middle East energy shock is the source of the supply constraints affecting households and firms.
Trump administration tariff increases through executive orders, given expected U.S. legislative gridlock in 2027.
EU safeguard measures on Chinese chemicals, which could extend to machinery and furniture.
France's fiscal and political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential elections has lifted spreads to levels not seen since the 2012 eurozone crisis.
U.S.-China competition for AI dominance, with China unlikely to slow AI investment if the U.S. does.
Political resistance to data center development could delay projects.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings are strong, estimates are rising, cloud growth is accelerating and compute capacity is sold out. Data center capex is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Investors question returns on invested capital. AI equities fell in Q3 2026, and financing circularity, hyperscaler issuance and political resistance to data centers add risk.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A change in end demand, utilization or customer revenue growth, which PGIM says would be the key test. It currently sees these indicators as constructive.

tension_points.bull_case: U.S. equity returns have shown low sensitivity to rising Treasury yields, and high yield and EM debt excess returns have been positive when yields rose.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher funding costs and rarely expanding P/E ratios when the Fed hikes, plus a recession probability that rises to near 25%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A slowdown in the U.S. economy or Fed overtightening causing negative demand shocks.
